# Install

How to install pysacd from PyPI, check a download, and build it from source on Linux, macOS and
Windows.

## From PyPI

Python 3.10 or later. There are wheels for:

| System | Wheel |
|---|---|
| Linux, glibc 2.28 or later | x86-64 and aarch64 (manylinux) |
| Linux, musl 1.2 or later | x86-64 (musllinux) |
| macOS 11 or later | arm64 (Apple Silicon) |
| macOS 10.13 or later | x86-64 (Intel) |
| Windows | x86-64 |

Anywhere else, pip builds from source ([below](#from-source)). The macOS wheels are built for
those versions and run-tested on macOS 15 only (arm64 and x86-64). On macOS 11 to 14 they are
untested, so please report how they do there.

```sh
pip install pysacd                    # engine, libFLAC and mutagen included
pysacd --version                      # shows how the engine was built
```

Wheels are portable builds: the PCM conversion picks its SIMD level when it runs, with the same
output on every CPU.

## Checking a download

The same files are on each [GitHub release](https://github.com/aclater/pysacd/releases), each
with its build provenance attestation beside it as `<file>.intoto.jsonl`. Check a wheel with
the GitHub CLI:

```sh
gh attestation verify pysacd-0.5.5-py3-none-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl --repo aclater/pysacd
```

To check offline against the attached bundle, add
`--bundle pysacd-0.5.5-py3-none-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl.intoto.jsonl`.

## From source

On Linux or macOS, the build needs a C compiler and make, Rust (cargo 1.83 or later), and libFLAC
for FLAC output. The build compiles the [dsd2pcm](https://github.com/aclater/dsd2pcm-rs) C library,
which converts DSD to PCM, from the release source pinned in `dsd2pcm.lock`, checked by its SHA-256.
On a machine without Rust, this installs the pinned Rust release into `build/rust` of the source
tree; then put the `build/rust/bin` folder it prints on your PATH for the build:

```sh
python3 tools/dsd2pcm.py toolchain --dest build/rust
```

The build downloads the [scarletbook-rs](https://github.com/aclater/scarletbook-rs) C library
that the engine links, from its GitHub release, and checks it against the SHA-256 pinned in
`scarletbook.lock`. To build offline, see
[development](../development.md#the-scarletbook-library).

```sh
# Fedora/RHEL: sudo dnf install gcc make flac-devel
# Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt install gcc make libflac-dev pkg-config
# macOS (Homebrew): brew install flac pkg-config   (clang comes with the Xcode tools)
git clone https://github.com/aclater/pysacd && cd pysacd
pip install -e '.[convert]'                  # builds a portable engine
make                                         # optional: rebuild it for this CPU
```

`PYSACD_NATIVE=1 pip install .` builds for this CPU from the start.

## Windows from source

Build the engine with MSYS2's UCRT64 toolchain. It links statically, so the DLL needs nothing
beside it, and works with the normal python.org Python:

```sh
# with your Python, from any shell: the scarletbook library the engine links (pinned, checked)
python tools/scarletbook.py fetch --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu --dest build/scarletbook
# in an MSYS2 UCRT64 shell
pacman -S make mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-pkgconf mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-flac
make                                          # builds src/pysacd/_sacdconv.dll
# then, from any shell with your Python
pip install -e '.[convert]' --no-build-isolation
```

On Windows, `pysacd convert` always uses Windows-safe file names.
